talks.title: From Printers to Silver Tickets or Something
talks.teaser: Demonstrates pivoting from compromised networked printers into Active Directory environments to forge Kerberos silver tickets.
talks.summary:
Evil Mog from Team Hashcat and X-Force Red demonstrates an end-to-end Active Directory exploitation chain starting from an insecure network printer and escalating all the way to Kerberos Silver Tickets and domain credential dumping. He explains how embedded devices like network multifunction printers frequently store unencrypted LDAP service account credentials or permit simple bind capture when reconfigured to point to an attacker-controlled service.

The presentation walks through extracting cached credentials, identifying service principal names (SPNs), and formatting captured hashes for high-speed cracking with Hashcat. At 02:58, Evil Mog demonstrates configuring target service accounts and executing ticket requests. He details using Impacket tools at 08:22 and 09:48 to forge Silver Tickets with specific service rights, ultimately executing `secretsdump.py` (11:01) against domain controllers to harvest Active Directory domain hashes without generating domain-wide Golden Ticket alerts.

talks.title: Getting Started with Hashcat (Stream Session)
talks.teaser: A walkthrough demonstrating core Hashcat attack modes, rule manipulation, and dictionary optimization.
talks.summary:
Security practitioner PNI leads a hands-on instructional workshop in the Password Village, demonstrating how to install, configure, and operate Hashcat on an NVIDIA GPU workstation to perform high-speed password cracking [00:00]. PNI guides viewers through downloading Hashcat, importing and verifying developer GPG signing keys, configuring the NVIDIA CUDA toolkit, and updating system path configurations (`ld.so.conf.d`) to ensure optimal GPU acceleration [03:28, 08:32].

The presentation covers the fundamental syntax and attack modes of Hashcat. PNI demonstrates running straight dictionary attacks (`-a 0`) using classic wordlists like RockYou against Windows NT hashes (`-m 1000`) captured from penetration tests and Responder LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning attacks [12:49]. He explains how to interpret Hashcat's console status display, including candidate speed metrics, GPU temperature monitoring, device utilization, restore checkpointing, and cracked hash recovery rates [16:12].

PNI illustrates how GPU acceleration drastically reduces cracking time, demonstrating Hashcat evaluating candidates at over 5.8 billion hashes per second and rapidly cracking nearly 45% of the target sample set in seconds [19:44]. The session concludes with practical tips on rule-based attacks, mask-based brute forcing, and foundational concepts for attendees following along with advanced Password Village sessions [23:41].

talks.title: Practical PCFG Password Cracking
talks.teaser: Explains how Probabilistic Context-Free Grammars (PCFGs) model human password creation patterns to generate highly effective cracking guesses.
talks.summary:
Matt Weir presents practical applications of Probabilistic Context-Free Grammars (PCFG) for advanced password cracking. He contrasts traditional dictionary and brute-force approaches against structural grammar analysis, explaining how human password creation follows predictable linguistic, semantic, and keyboard patterns that can be modeled probabilistically to generate highly targeted guess lists.

Weir discusses the internal mechanics of the open-source PCFG toolset at 12:11, explaining how training sets transform into probabilistic grammar rules combining base words, character replacements, and digit appendages. At 17:56 and 21:04, he demonstrates optimizing rule generation and evaluating metric coverage (24:02) to maximize cracking efficiency while minimizing duplicate guesses (40:03). He emphasizes tuning training corpora against target organizations (37:04) to crack complex corporate passwords that standard wordlists miss.

talks.title: Practical PCFG Password Cracking Q&A
talks.teaser: Dr. Matt Weir answers community questions on PCFG trainer implementation, grammar tuning, and real-world hash list cracking.
talks.summary:
In this Password Village Q&A session, researcher Matt Weir answers community questions regarding Probabilistic Context-Free Grammar (PCFG) password cracking and the structural modeling of human-generated passwords [00:00]. Weir explains that while traditional brute-force and Markov-chain tools treat passwords as random byte sequences or character n-grams, PCFG decodes passwords into semantic grammatical structures—such as base structures consisting of alphabetic root words, capitalization patterns, special characters, and numeric digit sequences [04:30].

Weir details how the PCFG trainer parses large public credential dumps to learn replacement probability distributions, allowing cracking engines to prioritize high-probability human mnemonic structures before attempting low-yield combinatorial patterns [09:15]. He compares PCFG performance against modern rule-based engines in Hashcat and John the Ripper, noting that while GPU-accelerated rule evaluation is faster in raw guesses per second, PCFG's superior guess efficiency frequently recovers complex corporate passwords in fewer total attempts [14:40].

The session covers practical guidance on training custom grammars against target-specific password policies and organizational leaks [19:20]. Weir addresses computational overhead, memory management when loading extensive grammars, and strategies for combining PCFG output with GPU-based mask pipelines for maximum effectiveness in red team and audit environments [24:10].

talks.title: Cracking at Extreme Scale
talks.teaser: Jeremi Gosney discusses building and managing multi-GPU supercomputing clusters engineered for massive-scale password recovery.
talks.summary:
Jeremi Gosney breaks down the engineering challenges and architecture required to build and operate massive GPU password-cracking clusters at extreme scale. Drawing on years of designing high-performance computing clusters, he details the physical, thermal, electrical, and hardware pitfalls encountered when scaling from single multi-GPU rigs to distributed multi-node clusters.

Gosney covers driver configuration headaches and OpenCL kernel execution nuances across heterogeneous GPU architectures at 13:10 and 26:25. He explores the software layer at 20:55, explaining the necessity of distributed job scheduling, hashlist distribution across nodes, workload balancing, and fault tolerance when individual GPU cards crash or overheat. At 32:00, he describes automated remote cluster provisioning, monitoring frameworks, and managing multi-tenant cluster access without compromising security or job integrity.
